In our study, we identified several challenges that could contribute to further optimization and implementation of Watson in clinical practice. Clinical decision support systems are typically evaluated in clinical trials, and evaluate whether the system changes the pro¬cess of care in ways which could affect clinical outcomes [ ]. However, before determining whether advice is followed, it is first necessary to ensure that the system is providing the right advice. As outlined in the introduction, this is typically done by first comparing the system to the clinical knowledge on which it was based, then comparing the output of the system to the judg¬ment of clinical experts in a defined set of test cases. In Watson and other neural network systems, there is no specification to perform this first step. Thus, following the recommendations of Smith et al.[ ], we have chosen to compare to another system. Oncoguide is intended to represent the standard of evidence-based care in The Netherlands (as it is a representation of the Dutch colorectal cancer guidelines in decision trees), thus it is a logical choice for evaluating the system for use in The Nether¬lands [ ]. Comparison against an objective standard also adds value over only comparing with clinician judgment [ ]. Given the large number of test cases we expect to generate, this also allows us to perform the evaluation more efficiently, as we can reasonably assume that if Watson and Oncoguide agree then the clinician will also agree. In many respects, a machine learning system can be viewed as a prediction model: the system "pre¬dicts" which treatment experts would recommend for this pa¬tient. Thus this evaluation can also be viewed as an "external validation" of this model: US-based experts trained the system, and it is not known if its recommendations will be valid in an-other setting. This protocol introduces two new methods for evaluating ar¬tificial intelligence-based decision support systems: a method for generating synthetic cases, and the scoring system for as¬sessing agreement. Synthetic cases are generated based on the known inputs and outputs of the comparison system (in our ex¬ample, Oncoguide), and input from clinical experts on variables, which might indicate a justifiable departure from the guideline. This approach should capture both cases where Watson is likely to agree with the guideline, and cases where Watson may be able to offer better advice than the guideline. As with other decision support systems, simple "agreement" is not sufficient to describe the performance of this system [ ]. Friedman and Wyatt pro¬posed the use of contingency tables when evaluating decision support systems, to make explicit the difference between false positive and false negative classifications. Their reasoning is that a false-positive error, such as erroneously suggesting a di¬agnosis for a healthy patient, may be less serious than a false-negative error, which may in turn be less serious than proposing the wrong diagnosis entirely [ ]. Likewise, a suggestion from the system that the clinician "consider" a treatment, which is in fact contraindicated, is a less serious error than "recommend¬ing" use of that treatment. Thus, we have extended the notion of a contingency table to express the idea that some disagreements have greater consequences than others. Preliminary results from other concordance studies with Watson appear in the literature, primarily in conference proceed¬ings. Oncologists at Bumrungrad International Hospital in Thai¬land compared Watson's recommendations to the recommenda¬tions of their own oncologists [ ]. They found 89% concor¬dance for colorectal cancer patients, which is substantially better than concordance levels in our feasibility study. An earlier study in India reported 81.0% concordance for colon and 92.7% con¬cordance for rectal cancer [ ]. A study in South Korea found 85% concordance for colon cancer in the adjuvant setting [ ]. Although thus far these studies have only been reported in ab¬stract format, the reported methods suggest three possible rea¬sons for the differences. First, these studies used real patients, which (as discussed below) is a different outcome than in our study. Second, they used a simple definition of concordance: if the treatment selected by oncologists appeared in either the 'recommended' or 'for consideration' part of Watson's advice, then the recommendation was considered concordant. By con-trast, our approach allows for different levels of disagreement: if Watson recommends a treatment that is contraindicated by the Dutch or NCCN guideline, that is a more substantial disagree¬ment than simply not mentioning a treatment recommended by our guideline, or suggesting a treatment "for consideration" that the Dutch or NCCN guideline omits. Our approach captures and quantifies this difference. Finally, the guidelines used in these countries may more closely parallel US guidelines. In the Ko¬rean

if the treatment selected by oncologists appeared in either the 'recommended' or 'for consideration' part of Watson's advice, then the recommendation was considered concordant. By con-trast, our approach allows for different levels of disagreement: if Watson recommends a treatment that is contraindicated by the Dutch or NCCN guideline, that is a more substantial disagree¬ment than simply not mentioning a treatment recommended by our guideline, or suggesting a treatment "for consideration" that the Dutch or NCCN guideline omits. Our approach captures and quantifies this difference. Finally, the guidelines used in these countries may more closely parallel US guidelines. In the Ko¬rean study it was noted that most of the observed disagreements were attributable to differences with the US guidelines. We performed an additional comparison of Watson versus the NCCN guidelines to gain a sense of the degree to which non-concordance between Watson and Oncoguide was attributable to non-concordance between Dutch and US guidelines. We iden¬tified variety in the concordance scores in both situations, but no orange or red flags were reported for the comparison be¬tween Watson and the NCCN guidelines. This supports that dis¬agreements between Watson and Oncoguide are (partially) at¬tributable to guideline differences. We chose to use synthetic cases rather than real cases to per¬form our evaluation, because our main goal was to detect differ¬ences between Watson's advice and our local guidelines. This means that our evaluation did not measure how often Watson's advice would agree with the guideline in practice and real pa¬tient cases. We attempted to create a heterogeneous dataset of synthetic patient cases to overcome this issue, but our dataset was still limited in terms of variation (e.g. age was restricted to 3 levels: 45, 60 and 75 years and kidney or liver diseases were present or absent). This was due the need to manually enter all cases. An easier way to import a larger dataset of patient cases is by using an application-programming interface (API), but this option was unfortunately not available in the timeframe of our study. If an API were to be provided for automated entry of (test) patient data, then we could exhaustively test of all possible com¬binations of variables, including continuous variables (e.g. per year for age and different levels of kidney and/or liver disease). We intend to repeat out study with patients with more compli¬cated features. We elected to use a simple, expert-based usability evalua-tion, the cognitive walkthrough approach. We considered this approach to be appropriate to the circumstances of this evalu-ation: the tasks to be accomplished in the system were well-defined, and the main goal was to identify usability issues that could be a barrier to use of the system in a trial setting with naive users [ ]. Furthermore, the interface itself is relatively simple, and more qualitative methods such as think-aloud were, in the authors' view, unlikely to yield additional insights. Although no usability problems were identified and the system is usable for our proposed evaluation, the workflow of hand-entering data is cumbersome. Direct interoperability with a patient record database would be preferable, but it is neither available for the electronic health record in use at our hospital nor for synthetic cases. In our study, we calculated overall concordance scores per case between Watson's advice and the Dutch guidelines and used orange and red flags to indicate differences in treatment recom¬mendations. However, we did not decide whether discordance is actually a positive or negative change regarding to the orig¬inal Dutch guideline recommendation. In other words, we did not conclude whether Watson's advice may be actually better or worse than the Dutch guideline recommendations. Future re¬search should therefore critically evaluate each case of discor¬dance, including evaluation by oncologists of the clinical sound¬ness of the recommendation and examining the literature refer¬ences Watson provides to see if they justify its recommendation. Future work could also include an assessment of whether the lit¬erature that Watson provides could in and of itself be of value to the decision-making process. Watson's approach of generating personalized treatment ad¬vice by integrating natural language processing with evidence from guidelines and studies, case-based reasoning, and machine learning based on training by expert oncologists is definitely promising in terms of revolutionizing daily clinical practice with the ongoing expansion of medical literature. Watson also has the potential to conquer two difficult problems from decision support perspective, namely that of poorly structured medical record data and maintaining the knowledge base. However, if further implementation of Watson outside the United States is being pursued, future research should focus on further evaluation after localization of Watson with adjustments based on national or local guidelines. "Black-box" systems such as Watson im¬pose a risk that other decision support systems do not, in that we cannot know exactly how the system arrives at its conclusions. For example, Oncoguide does not consider the patient s age in

medical literature. Watson also has the potential to conquer two difficult problems from decision support perspective, namely that of poorly structured medical record data and maintaining the knowledge base. However, if further implementation of Watson outside the United States is being pursued, future research should focus on further evaluation after localization of Watson with adjustments based on national or local guidelines. "Black-box" systems such as Watson im¬pose a risk that other decision support systems do not, in that we cannot know exactly how the system arrives at its conclusions. For example, Oncoguide does not consider the patient s age in its recommendations; its users are aware of this and compensate accordingly. Watson may or may not be considering age, and its end users have no way to know when it does, or whether this may change with a new version update. A partial solution could be to maintain a suite of test patients as we ve proposed in our protocol, and to run these tests regularly. Then clinicians could be made aware if its recommendations change for some groups of patients. In conclusion, a systematic evaluation of a "black-box" deci¬sion support tool is feasible using synthetic patient cases and em¬pirically testing the outcomes. Several reasons for discordance of a decision tool with synthetic cases should be considered, but disagreements were undoubtedly partially attributable to differ¬ences between the Dutch and US guidelines. This may imply that Watson needs to be re-trained by local experts to reflect dif¬ferences in the local care setting. Localization of a cognitive decision support tool (e.g. Watson) based on local guidelines is therefore essential before considering further external validity studies and implementation in daily practice.

documents.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology Rectal Cancer Surgical Management

chunks.content: Introduction: Concordance with evidence-based guidelines reduces care variation and improves outcomes. Guidelines are created using a rigorous process wherein a multidisciplinary panel of experts systematically reviews the literature, providing ratings of available evidence( ). National clinical guidelines, such as those produced by the National Comprehensive Cancer Care Network (NCCN), specify recommendations for evaluation, treatment, and surveillance of patients with colorectal cancer. The NCCN guidelines are developed by a panel of oncologic specialists through a continuous iterative process that provides critical best-practice updates to clinicians( , ). It has been shown for both colon and rectal cancer that concordance with NCCN guidelines reduces mortality( , ). Guidelines reduce variation of care by creating standardization. Variation has been identified as a driver of increased surgical mortality, and many quality improvement efforts are working to decrease variation across hospitals and providers ( ). Determining rates of concordance to cancer care guidelines is an important step in understanding current gaps in care and developing targeted system-wide quality implementation interventions. However, depending on the study and measures, guideline concordance in colon and rectal cancer may range from 22%−92%( – ). Variation in guideline concordance is related to which guideline is chosen, and current studies value all guidelines equally, i.e., ordering an appropriate laboratory test is equally valued when compared to receipt of chemotherapy. Facility designation as a cancer center or academic hospital affects guideline concordance( , ), however there is little information available regarding the impact of other facility-level characteristics as well as the geographical distribution of patients who receive and facilities who perform guideline concordant care. Addressing these gaps will allow for more targeted and effective interventions to reduce variation in colorectal cancer care. Facility-level and geographical variation can alter guideline concordance through modifiable processes. Our objectives were to 1) Examine rates of guideline non-concordance in a multi-hospital, geographically varied health system; 2) Examine factors associated with non-concordant care; and 3) Identify geographical patterns of non-concordant care for future quality improvement interventions. Methods: Study Population: A retrospective cohort of colorectal cancer patients diagnosed between 2011–2021 were identified from a 16-hospital health-system. We initially obtained records for 5859 patients from an institutional cancer registry maintained by trained registrars. We excluded patients who had missing insurance information, county of diagnosis, treatment center, and who were missing both clinical and pathologic staging information. We also excluded patients who did not have the following adenocarcinoma International Classification of Disease (ICD-0-3) histology codes: 8000/3, 8140, 8140/3, 8144/3, 8210/2, 8210/3, 8211/3,8213/3, 8220/2, 8220/3, 8245/3, 8261/2, 8261/3, 8262/3, 8263/2, 8263/3, 8480/3, 8481/3. Finally, we excluded patients who had stage IV disease, who had appendiceal or rectosigmoid locations of their cancer, who were older than 85 years, or if the patient refused treatment. There was no missingness for surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, CEA, and MSI variables. There was 1 patient with missing lymph node harvest (0.04%) and 6 patients with missing margin (0.26%) data. Sensitivity analysis was conducted, and the results were not changed with or without inclusion of patients who were missing data for margins and lymph node harvest. ( .) This study was deemed Exempt by the Indiana University IRB (IRB# 18804.) Guideline Non-Concordance: Quality indicators were developed and adapted from the most recent guidelines for the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and similar studies ( , , ). Major criteria concordance for colon cancer includes surgery without radiation or chemotherapy for stage I disease, surgery without radiation for stage II disease, and surgery with chemotherapy and without radiation for stage III disease. Major criteria concordance for rectal cancer includes surgery without radiation or chemotherapy for stage I disease, and surgery with radiation and chemotherapy for both stage II and stage III disease. Minor criteria concordance includes ordering CEA and MSI laboratory tests as well as documenting cancer margins and lymph node harvest after surgery ( .) Groups were created for complete guideline concordance (an absence of guideline non-concordance), minor-only quality indicator guideline non-concordance (MIN), and major quality indicator guideline non-concordance (MAJ). Patients’ demographics were analyzed across guideline non-concordance groups to determine non-concordance rates. Demographics included age, gender, race and ethnicity, and health insurance. Education and income were examined using data from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality Social Determinants of Health Database that utilize data from multiple sources across key social determinants of health such as social, economic, education, physical infrastructure, and healthcare( ). Metro designation of county of residence was examined and determined with Rural Urban Continuum Codes, designations created by the National Center for Health Statistics separating counties into three metro categories based on population, and six non-metro categories based on urbanization and adjacency to metro counties ( ). Anatomical location of the cancer was limited to colon or rectum. Staging information prioritized the highest clinical or pathologic stage that was available. Patient use of unique hospital networks

Health Database that utilize data from multiple sources across key social determinants of health such as social, economic, education, physical infrastructure, and healthcare( ). Metro designation of county of residence was examined and determined with Rural Urban Continuum Codes, designations created by the National Center for Health Statistics separating counties into three metro categories based on population, and six non-metro categories based on urbanization and adjacency to metro counties ( ). Anatomical location of the cancer was limited to colon or rectum. Staging information prioritized the highest clinical or pathologic stage that was available. Patient use of unique hospital networks and location of these facilities was analyzed. Hospital networks were determined by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality in the 2021 Compendium of US Health Systems, which documents physicians and hospitals that are connected through common ownership or joint management( ). Traveling during cancer care was examined with Surveillance Epidemiology and End Result (SEER) Hospital Service Areas (HSA), which are counties or areas that are self-contained regions for patients to seek hospital care. Indiana county heat maps were created examining relationships between a patients’ county of residence at the time of diagnosis and predictors of MAJ non-concordance( ). Proportions of MAJ non-concordance and patients with greater than 60 days from diagnosis to treatment were determined for each county. Population total and age adjusted weighted rates were calculated for each county with data from the United States Census Bureau( , ). Higher quartiles of the adjusted rates indicate increased MAJ non-concordance and greater than 60 days from diagnosis to treatment respectively. Statistical Analysis: Continuous data were analyzed using Mann-Whitney test. Categorical data were analyzed using χ2 test or Fisher exact test where appropriate. One way ANOVA or Kruskal Wallis test were used for continuous data where appropriate. Kolmogorov–Smirnov test and the Shapiro–Wilk test was conducted to determine normality. Cases with missing information were excluded. Binary logistic regression was conducted with all variables from the unadjusted analysis. These variables were determined from similar studies( , ). The outcome of interest was receipt of MAJ non-concordant care. All analysis was performed with STATA Version 18 (College Station, TX: StataCorp LLC) and R Version 4.3.0 (Vienna, Austria: R Foundation for Statistical Computing.) Results: Overview: Rates of Guideline Non-Concordance: Overall, we identified 2324 patients between 2011–2021 who had colon (68.2%, n=1585) or rectal cancer (31.8%, n=739) that received care within a large health-system and met inclusion criteria. There was a complete guideline-concordance (an absence of guideline non-concordance) rate of 24.7% (n=573), MIN non-concordance rate of 63.3% (n=1471), and MAJ non-concordance rate of 12.4% (n=280) ( .) Patients who received MAJ non-concordant care were predominately male (62.9%), identified as white (87.9%), and had a median age of 66 years (Interquartile range 55.5–76.) Most patients who received MAJ non-concordant care were insured by Medicare (58.2%). Examination of zip code level data revealed that those who were diagnosed in a metro county (68.2%) were most often to receive MAJ non-concordant care. Examination of hospital networks revealed that most patients who received MAJ non-concordant care had used one hospital network (79.3%) and obtained all of their cancer care within one SEER HSA (55.0%). Patients with rectal cancer (56.8%) and stage III cancer (61.1%) were the most common anatomic location and cancer stage for MAJ non-concordant care respectively. Among the 280 MAJ non-concordant patients, the most common reason for non-concordance among colon cancer patients was not receiving chemotherapy for stage III disease (29.3%, n=82) and the most common reason for non-concordance among rectal cancer patients were non-concordant with two or more major treatments (24.3%, n=68) ( ). Factors Associated with MAJ Non-Concordance: Among the 2324 identified patients, 280 (12.4%) received MAJ non-concordant care. After adjusting for all variables in and stratifying by anatomic cancer location, colon cancer patients were more likely to receive MAJ non-concordant care if they had stage II (OR=3.10, CI 1.21–7.96) or stage III cancer (OR=22.07, CI 9.43–51.70,) if they had greater than 1 Charleson-Deyo Comorbidity Index score (1.66 OR 1.05–2.64,) or if they took longer than 60 days after diagnosis to receive their first cancer treatment (OR=3.04, CI 1.58–5.85.) Colon cancer patients were less likely to receive MAJ non-concordant care if they received care from >1 hospital network (OR=0.47, CI 0.24–0.91) ( ). Rectal cancer patients were significantly more likely to receive MAJ non-concordant care if they took longer than 60 days after diagnosis to receive their first cancer treatment (OR=2.73, CI 1.76–4.22). Rectal cancer patients were less likely to receive MAJ non-concordant care if they used >1 unique facilities for their cancer treatment (OR=0.49, CI 0.31–0.77) ( ). Notably, there was not a significant relationship with median income or high school education and MAJ non-concordance for both colon and rectal cancer patients. Similarly, there was not a significant relationship with rurality and SEER HSA

>1 hospital network (OR=0.47, CI 0.24–0.91) ( ). Rectal cancer patients were significantly more likely to receive MAJ non-concordant care if they took longer than 60 days after diagnosis to receive their first cancer treatment (OR=2.73, CI 1.76–4.22). Rectal cancer patients were less likely to receive MAJ non-concordant care if they used >1 unique facilities for their cancer treatment (OR=0.49, CI 0.31–0.77) ( ). Notably, there was not a significant relationship with median income or high school education and MAJ non-concordance for both colon and rectal cancer patients. Similarly, there was not a significant relationship with rurality and SEER HSA visited during cancer treatment. Geographical Predictors of MAJ Non-Concordance: Among 92 Indiana counties there were 74 counties that included data for colon cancer patients while there were 75 counties that included data for rectal cancer patients. After adjusting for census population and age distribution of the patient’s county of diagnosis, the highest quartiles of MAJ non-concordance and time to treatment were found in Marion County (location of Indianapolis and RUCC designation as a metro area of 1 million population) for both colon and rectal cancer ( ). Discussion: Colorectal cancer care requires coordination of multiple providers for patient care, frequently across various locations. Guideline concordance is crucial to improve quality and patient outcomes. We found that the majority of colorectal patients within our large health system receive major quality indicator treatment modalities such as surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation. Patients who receive MAJ non-concordant care are more likely to wait longer for their treatment, which may drive non-concordance. For both colon and rectal cancer, the largest adjusted rates of these patients are located in a single county. Despite the majority of state-wide healthcare resources existing within this county, MAJ non-concordance may occur within these large centers, which treat patients from the most populated county, the entire state, and neighboring states, potentially leading to increased patient volumes and treatment delays. Localization of this hotspot of MAJ non-concordance will allow for targeted quality improvement interventions that ultimately improve guideline concordance within this health-system and state-wide. Guideline concordance rates focus on a variety of quality indicators and are variable. Rates of concordance with major treatment modalities for colon and rectal cancer such as surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation typically range between 50–90% ( – ). Likewise, rates of concordance with quality indicators that were not major treatment modalities can range from 22%−92%( – ). Our study has found that 12.4% of patients within a large health system received MAJ guideline non-concordant care. Rates of MAJ non-concordance were 7.6% for colon cancer and 21.5% for rectal cancer. However, only 24.7% of patients received complete guideline concordant (an absence of guideline non-concordance) care with 63.3% of patients receiving MIN non-concordance due to missing laboratory tests or surgical documentation. Previous studies fail to distinguish a difference between the significance of the guideline measured to determine concordance. Although all guidelines are important, receipt of treatment provides a critical influence on a patient’s outcome while a missing laboratory value can be less consequential. The most common reasons for MAJ non-concordance among rectal cancer patients were greater than one MAJ non-concordant treatments and not receiving surgery. These patients were spread across all stages with various combinations of missing major quality indicators. In our analysis, rectal cancer was also significantly more likely to result in MAJ non-concordance compared to colon cancer. Rectal cancer requires multimodal therapy more often resulting in greater complexity. Care providers for patients with rectal cancer have a greater burden to maintain current knowledge as innovative approaches to rectal cancer emerge( – ). These providers may benefit from tools that provide education for current NCCN guidelines, as new iterations may contain more changes than other similar cancer types. Colon cancer patients who were MAJ non-concordant were most frequently due to not receiving chemotherapy for stage III cancers. Others have found high rates of chemotherapy non-concordance for stage III colon cancer ranging from 29% to 51% ( – ). These patients may have had prolonged recovery due to complications following their operation, delaying or otherwise precluding the ability to give chemotherapy, which has been well described( , ). Of the stage III colon cancer patients we studied, only 14.5% exhibited MAJ non-concordance due to not receiving chemotherapy, suggesting a high level of overall concordance among the cohort. Identification of predictors for MAJ non-concordance is critical to improve concordance rates. We found that colon cancer patients had increased odds of MAJ non-concordance with increased comorbidities. Others have found a similar relationship with increased comorbidities and non-concordance( – ). Complex comorbid patients may be unable to tolerate standard guideline recommended care and require more nuanced care, which deviates from guidelines. Optimization of comorbidities prior to initiation of treatment may allow for patients to follow standard guideline pathways. Many studies examine hospital level

MAJ non-concordance due to not receiving chemotherapy, suggesting a high level of overall concordance among the cohort. Identification of predictors for MAJ non-concordance is critical to improve concordance rates. We found that colon cancer patients had increased odds of MAJ non-concordance with increased comorbidities. Others have found a similar relationship with increased comorbidities and non-concordance( – ). Complex comorbid patients may be unable to tolerate standard guideline recommended care and require more nuanced care, which deviates from guidelines. Optimization of comorbidities prior to initiation of treatment may allow for patients to follow standard guideline pathways. Many studies examine hospital level factors and relationship with guideline non-concordance such as hospital volume, teaching status, Commission on Cancer (CoC) accreditation, National Cancer Institute designation, and safety net status ( , , , , – ). Results from these studies indicate improved care and outcomes for hospitals that have increased volume, academic teaching status, and meet cancer accreditation standards. When examining surgical outcomes and hospital network affiliation, there was no difference between network and non-network affiliated hospitals( ). Cancer guideline non-concordance has also been found to be similar between network and non-network hospitals at baseline( ). All of these previous works must be interpreted with caution as they involve different guidelines to determine concordance and outcomes measured. In our study, colon cancer patients were less likely to receive MAJ non-concordant care if they used >1 hospital network. Utilization of multiple hospital networks allows providers with fresh perspectives on the patients’ case to offer input and second-opinions. If a multidisciplinary team in one hospital network opts for MAJ non-concordant care, this decision may be corrected by a multidisciplinary team in a second network. Patients with private insurance who pay higher premiums have access to increased physician network breadth and hospital network breadth( ). While patients with private insurance and higher income may have had more resources to utilize >1 hospital network and thereby experience less MAJ non-concordant care, we found no significant association with insurance type or median household income. Although time to treatment has been studied as it relates to survival, there is little evidence of its impact on guideline concordance( ). We found increased odds of MAJ non-concordance for both colon and rectal cancer with increased time from diagnosis to treatment. As time to treatment increases, there are increased opportunities for patients to be lost to follow up or experience progression of their disease. This is the type of potentially actionable information that will inform future efforts. For example, patients with confirmed diagnoses and without documented evaluations with a provider over a certain day threshold (e.g., 30 or 60 days) might be targeted with several patient- and provider-facing interventions to improve timely follow-up. Immediate identification and contact of patients experiencing extended time to treatment can prevent loss to follow up and improve guideline concordance. Increased time to treatment may be a process failure( ), therefore evaluation and referral could be more efficient to alleviate this issue. Others have found that care fragmentation leads to increased time to treatment, however there is little evidence relating care fragmentation or increased time to treatment to guideline concordance( ). We found that patients who were in non-metro locations and traveled to more than one health service area for care were not significantly more likely to receive MAJ non-concordant care in our cohort. Similarly, there is evidence on the utilization of multiple facilities for colorectal cancer care affecting survival, but there is no available evidence relating to guideline concordance( , ). We found that rectal cancer patients who use >1 facility for care are less likely to receive MAJ non-concordant care. Stage II and stage III rectal cancer require complex care with 3 treatment modalities required to avoid MAJ non-concordance. Patients who travel to multiple facilities likely sought up to 3 treatment modalities, thereby avoiding MAJ non-concordance. Likewise, those who only went to one facility may reflect the fact that they did not receive a MAJ treatment modality. Colon cancer had increased odds of MAJ non-concordance for stage II and stage III disease compared to stage I, which aligns with previous literature ( ). Stage II and stage III colon cancer care is increasingly complex compared to stage I, which may account for this difference in MAJ non-concordance. Due to limitations of data sources, it is difficult to identify counties where non-concordance occurs. Investigation of health service areas in Texas has provided distributions of non-concordance, but this lacks the granularity of county-level analysis( ). We have identified Marion County, the location of Indianapolis, and most populated county in Indiana, as having the highest proportions of MAJ non-concordance and longer time to treatment. Identification of this pattern persists after adjusting for county population and age distribution. When considering that use of more than one care network was not significantly

Investigation of health service areas in Texas has provided distributions of non-concordance, but this lacks the granularity of county-level analysis( ). We have identified Marion County, the location of Indianapolis, and most populated county in Indiana, as having the highest proportions of MAJ non-concordance and longer time to treatment. Identification of this pattern persists after adjusting for county population and age distribution. When considering that use of more than one care network was not significantly associated with non-concordance, intervention within our health system, which has a large footprint in Marion County, is well positioned to address MAJ non-concordance. Limitations: This study has several limitations. First, as with any retrospective studies, there may be errors in collection or recording of data. We found missingness among clinical and pathologic staging, which resulted in staging that selected the highest available stage from the data that was present. This may cause poor capture of upstaged and downstaged patients. Second, this study specifically examines one health system within Indiana. The health system examined in this study is the largest in Indiana, with many facilities spread around the entire state, and likely provides an accurate representation of our population of interest. Third, our dataset did not include several indicators to determine low and high risk stage II cancers. In response, we made concordance measures generous in favor of achieving concordance. Finally, it may be difficult to understand the exact reason that a patient received guideline non-concordant care from registry data as data fields do not allow for additional explanation by the provider, which is a common limitation in similar studies (4,7,9–11,21–23.) In future studies, we plan to conduct qualitative interviews with providers to address this challenge. Conclusion: The majority of colon and rectal cancer patients in a large health system received guideline concordant care, however 12% of patients received MAJ non-concordant care. Rectal cancer patients who had MAJ non-concordant care were most commonly due to missing more than two MAJ indicators and colon cancer patients were most commonly due to missing chemotherapy for treatment of stage III disease. Patients who had increased time to treatment had increased odds of MAJ non-concordance for both colon and rectal cancer. Improvement in efforts to ensure timely treatment may address non-concordance for both colon and rectal cancer. An identifiable location with the highest rates of non-concordance serves as a target for future quality improvement. Supplementary Material 1 2

chunks.content: Background Pancreatic cancer poses a great threat to human health, ranking 12th in global incidence and 6th in mortality among malignancies and causing over 460,000 deaths annually [ ]. Partial pancreatectomy is the primary curative treatment for focal pancreatic and periampullary lesions, particularly malignancies [ , ]. However, this procedure is challenging, with complication rates reaching 58%–80% and peri-operative mortality rates up to 17% [ – ]. Post-operative pancreatic fistula (POPF) is one of the most common and critical complications following partial pancreatectomy, occurring in up to 45% [ , ] and significantly increases the risk of other complications, including infections and hemorrhage, as well as mortality, which can double due to POPF [ – ]. Pre-operative prediction of POPF is of utmost interest, which can influence the choice of treatment and the evaluation of prognosis in patients with pancreatic and periampullary lesions. Previous studies indicated that the risk factors of POPF included old age, male sex, obesity, small diameter of the pancreatic duct, and soft pancreas tissue [ , – ]. Particularly, pancreas stiffness was thought to be one of the key factors associated with POPF [ – ]. Currently, intra-operative texture, magnetic resonance elastography, endoscopic ultrasound elastography, and pancreatic parenchymal fibrosis evaluation were used to assess pancreas stiffness and were shown to be associated with POPF occurrence [ , – ]. However, magnetic resonance elastography is expensive; endoscopic ultrasound elastography is technically complex; pancreatic fibrosis and texture assessment are difficult to evaluate pre-operatively and lack objective quantification. Thus, a non-invasive, objective, quantitative, and widely accessible method for pre-operative pancreas stiffness assessment remains to be explored. Two-dimensional shear wave elastography (2D-SWE) is a non-invasive method to understand tissue stiffness. While 2D-SWE is widely used in organs, including the liver and thyroid, its application in the pancreas remains limited [ – ]. Previous studies indicated pancreatic 2D-SWE measurement value‘s association with POPF [ , – ]. Other studies have also demonstrated the correlation between 2D-SWE measurement value and histological features such as pancreatic fibrosis [ – ], indicating its potential for predicting POPF by non-invasively assessing pancreatic histology. However, large-scale studies are still scarce, and the histological basis for using pancreatic 2D-SWE to predict POPF remains to be explored. Additionally, since the incidence of POPF varies across different types of surgeries, the application of 2D-SWE in predicting POPF in different surgery approaches requires further investigation [ , ]. The present study aimed to explore the feasibility and histological basis of pancreatic 2D-SWE measurement value in predicting POPF following partial pancreatectomy, and to build a prediction model of POPF by pre-operative features. Materials and methods Ethics The protocol of this single-center study was approved by the Institutional Review Board, and the written informed consent of the patients was collected before the data analysis. Patients enrollment From August 2023 to August 2024, 305 patients with pancreatic or periampullary diseases and undergoing partial pancreatectomy were prospectively enrolled (Fig. ). The patients were randomly divided into a training group ( n = 203) and a validation group ( n = 102). (Post hoc evaluation indicated an events-per-variable of 43, supporting the adequacy of the sample size.) The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≥ 18 years; (2) treatment-naïve pancreatic or periampullary diseases; (3) prepared to undergo partial pancreatectomy; (4) collected pre-operative data within one week before the surgery, including pancreatic 2D-SWE measurement. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) history of any pancreas-related treatment, including surgery, radiotherapy, or neoadjuvant therapy; (2) history of upper abdominal surgery or systemic treatment; (3) current acute phase of pancreatitis; (4) history of other malignancy; (5) history of severe systemic diseases, including acquired immunodeficiency syndrome; (6) inability to cooperate with pre-operative examinations or the surgery due to severe mental illness, cardiopulmonary dysfunction, or other reasons; (7) failure to obtain a valid 2D-SWE measurement. Pancreatic 2D-SWE measurement The pancreatic 2D-SWE examination was performed by the Aplio i900 ultrasound system (Canon Medical Systems, Japan) with the i8CX1 convex array probe (frequency 1.8–6.2 MHz). The examination was randomly conducted by five radiologists, each with over 3 years and more than 100 cases of pancreatic 2D-SWE examination experience. All patients fasted for at least 8 h before the examination. A comprehensive upper abdominal ultrasound examination was first performed. Then, the key acquisition parameters of 2D-SWE measurement were set as follows: Preferred site: Pancreatic body whenever feasible; head or tail used if the body was affected by any reasons and unsuitable for imaging, with the head preferred when both were measurable. Sampling frame: Placed in a clear parenchymal region ≥ 1 cm from the lesion, avoiding bowel gas, vessels > 3 mm, and any dilated duct. Imaging depth: 8 cm (adjusted within a range of 5–16 cm if necessary). Region of interest (ROI): Diameter 8 mm. Elasticity scale: 0–40 kPa. Patient position: Supine,

abdominal ultrasound examination was first performed. Then, the key acquisition parameters of 2D-SWE measurement were set as follows: Preferred site: Pancreatic body whenever feasible; head or tail used if the body was affected by any reasons and unsuitable for imaging, with the head preferred when both were measurable. Sampling frame: Placed in a clear parenchymal region ≥ 1 cm from the lesion, avoiding bowel gas, vessels > 3 mm, and any dilated duct. Imaging depth: 8 cm (adjusted within a range of 5–16 cm if necessary). Region of interest (ROI): Diameter 8 mm. Elasticity scale: 0–40 kPa. Patient position: Supine, probe aligned parallel to the transverse plane. Breath-hold: 3–5 s during acquisition. Quality control: Five consecutive, homogeneous frames with > 75% color fill; examination valid only if five measurements obtained and IQR/median < 30%. Measurement output: Median of five readings (Emean, kPa) and measurement site recorded.The above process was repeated five times. The examination was considered successful only if the five measurements were obtained and the interquartile range (IQR) to the median ratio was less than 30%. Then the median value of the five measurements (Emean, in kPa) and the site of measurement (pancreatic head, body, or tail) were recorded. Partial pancreatectomy The partial pancreatectomy was performed by a dedicated surgical team. The surgeons were divided according to their experience in pancreatic surgery as senior (with > 20 years of experience) and mid-level surgeons (with 10–20 years of experience). Partial pancreatectomy was categorized by the type of pancreatectomy into pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) and distal pancreatectomy (DP), and other surgeries (local excision of the lesion in any part of the pancreas), and by surgical technique into open surgery and minimally invasive surgery (including laparoscopic and Da Vinci robotic surgery). All patients underwent evaluation by a multidisciplinary medical team before the surgery. The surgeons and other peri-operative care personnel were blinded to the 2D-SWE measurement. According to the 2016 consensus of the International Study Group on Pancreatic Surgery (ISGPS) [ ], POPF was defined as amylase exceeding more than three times the upper limit of normal level (641 U/L at our center), measured in the drain fluid on or after the third post-operative day. POPF was graded as A (or biochemical leak), B, and C, and clinically-relevant POPF (CR-POPF) was referred to as POPF grades B and C. In this study, we used a broad definition of POPF (including grades A, B, and C) as the primary outcome for risk analysis, while also analysing CR-POPF and individual grades separately. POPF grading is detailed in Supplementary Table 1. Pancreatic histological features The interpretation of histological features was based on surgical specimens stained with hematoxylin and eosin after fixation in 10% formalin and paraffin embedding, with a section thickness of approximately 5 × 10 − 3 mm. The interpretation was performed by a pathologist with over 10 years of experience with a BX53 microscope (Olympus, Japan), and the eyepiece was adjusted to 10x magnification, while the objective lens was set to magnifications of 10-20x. The pathologist was blinded to the patients’ peri-operative conditions. For the lesion area, the lesion was categorized into benign lesions, malignant lesions, or neuroendocrine tumors. For the pancreatic parenchyma, a semi-quantitative histological assessment was performed (Supplementary Table 2), which included the degree of pancreatic fibrosis (F0-F3), lipomatosis (L0-L3), acinar atrophy (A0-A2), and stromal edema (E0-E3) [ , , ]. In 24 patients, there was insufficient volume of the non-lesion pancreatic parenchyma. For the correlation analysis between Emean and histological features, patients without available histological data for the non-lesion pancreatic parenchyma were excluded. While histological variables of all the patients were not included in the analysis of the multivariate logistic regression model, which was developed exclusively using pre-operative parameters. Data collection Patient characteristics, including demographics, serum laboratory analyses, imaging characteristics, histopathologic data, and surgical procedures, were collected. Pancreatic duct dilation was defined as the maximal internal diameter of the duct exceeding 3 mm on imaging. The location of the lesion was classified as pancreatic head, body, tail, or outside the pancreas. Lymph node metastasis and vascular invasion were determined based on the pathological diagnosis of the surgical resection specimens. Patients’ survival status was monitored for up to one month post-operatively. Statistical analysis Data were presented as mean (standard deviation), median [25th, 75th percentile], or frequency (percentage) as appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using the Student t -test or Mann-Whitney U test, while categorical variables were compared using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test as needed. The relationship between Emean and pancreatic conditions was analyzed using Spearman correlation analysis, and the discrimination ability was assessed by the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the area under the curve (AUC). The optimal ROC cutoffs were selected based on maximizing the Youden index, and sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values were calculated.

Data were presented as mean (standard deviation), median [25th, 75th percentile], or frequency (percentage) as appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using the Student t -test or Mann-Whitney U test, while categorical variables were compared using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test as needed. The relationship between Emean and pancreatic conditions was analyzed using Spearman correlation analysis, and the discrimination ability was assessed by the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the area under the curve (AUC). The optimal ROC cutoffs were selected based on maximizing the Youden index, and sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values were calculated. Patients were randomly assigned to the training or the validation group. Univariate and multivariate forward logistic regression analyses were used to explore the risk factors of POPF occurrence in the training group. Multivariate analyses were subsequently performed on the significant factors ( p < 0.050) in the univariate analyses. According to the multivariate analysis, a predictive model was built. Multicollinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors (VIF), with values < 2 considered acceptable. The goodness-of-fit of the model was assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test. Model performance was evaluated using AUC, calibration plots, Brier score, and calibration intercept and slope. Moreover, to assess potential overfitting and evaluate model robustness, a five-fold cross-validation was performed. The dataset was randomly partitioned into five subsets of approximately equal size. Each subset was sequentially used as a validation set, while the remaining four subsets served as the training set. The AUC was calculated for each fold, and the mean AUC with standard deviation was reported. Moreover, to evaluate the incremental predictive value of Emean, an Integrated Discrimination Improvement (IDI) analysis was performed by comparing the model with and without Emean. A two-sided p < 0.050 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics software version 26.0. (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY), MedCalc Statistical Software version 20.100 (MedCalc Software Ltd, Ostend, Belgium) and R software version 4.4.1. Results Patient characteristics Three hundred and five patients were enrolled in this study, with 157 (51.5%) males. The median age was 56.00 [44.00,66.00] years, and the median body mass index (BMI) was 22.43 [20.26, 24.48] kg/m². The median lesion size was 2.90 [2.00, 4.10] cm, with 120 (39.3%) cases located at the pancreatic head, while 52 (17.0%), 58 (19.0%), and 75 (24.6%) cases were located at the pancreatic body, tail, and other areas, respectively. The pancreatic duct was dilated in 88 (28.9%) patients. The median Emean was 7.00 [6.10, 8.50] kPa {or 1.53 [1.43, 1.68] m/s}, and 35 (11.5%) measurements were conducted at the pancreatic head and 270 (88.5%) at the body. Regarding the pancreatectomy type, 174 (57.0%) patients underwent PD, 106 (34.8%) underwent DP, and 25 (8.2%) underwent local excision of the lesion. As regards the surgical technique, 133 (43.6%) patients underwent open surgery and 172 (56.4%) underwent minimally invasive surgery [39 (12.8%) were laparoscopic and 133 (43.6%) were Da Vinci robotic surgery]. Among the surgeons, the senior surgeons performed 203 (66.6%) surgeries, while the mid-level surgeons performed 102 (33.4%). POPF occurred in 129 (42.3%) patients, with 75 (24.6%) at grade A (or biochemical leak). The occurrence rate of CR-POPF was 17.7%, including 40 (13.1%) in grade B and 14 (4.6%) in grade C. Three (1.0%) patients died within one month post-operatively, with two dying due to severe infections and POPF, and one dying from abdominal bleeding and non-infectious multiple organ failure. Aside from age ( p = 0.009), there were no significant differences in baseline characteristics between the two groups (all p > 0.050; Table ; Supplementary Table 3). Association between Emean and POPF Compared to the patient without POPF after partial pancreatectomy, Emean was lower in those with POPF {7.80 [6.65, 9.30] kPa vs. 6.30 [5.60, 7.00] kPa, p < 0.001}. According to ROC analysis of the entire cohort, Emean was significantly able to discriminate between the POPF occurrence {AUC [95% confidence interval (CI)] = 0.77 (0.72–0.83), cutoff (95% CI) = 7.34 (7.10–7.50) kPa, p < 0.001}. Emean’s discrimination to grade B [AUC (95% CI) = 0.80 (0.72–0.87), cutoff (95% CI) = 6.15 (5.60–7.10) kPa, p < 0.001] and grade C [AUC (95% CI) = 0.76 (0.62–0.89), cutoff (95% CI) = 6.15 (5.60–7.00.60.00) kPa, p < 0.001) was also significant, and as the POPF grade increased, the cutoff of Emean decreased (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 4). Histological basis of emean’s association with POPF In 24 patients, the non-lesion pancreatic parenchyma sample was insufficient for histological assessment, and these patients were excluded from the following histological correlation analysis. Compared with patients who had complete histological data, they showed differences in pre-operative carbohydrate antigen 125, red blood cell count, and type of pancreatectomy (all p < 0.050), while no significant differences were observed in other baseline characteristics (all p > 0.050; Supplementary Table 5). Emean

p < 0.001) was also significant, and as the POPF grade increased, the cutoff of Emean decreased (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 4). Histological basis of emean’s association with POPF In 24 patients, the non-lesion pancreatic parenchyma sample was insufficient for histological assessment, and these patients were excluded from the following histological correlation analysis. Compared with patients who had complete histological data, they showed differences in pre-operative carbohydrate antigen 125, red blood cell count, and type of pancreatectomy (all p < 0.050), while no significant differences were observed in other baseline characteristics (all p > 0.050; Supplementary Table 5). Emean was significantly correlated with pancreatic fibrosis ( r = 0.20, p < 0.001), acinar atrophy ( r = 0.15, p = 0.015), and stromal edema ( r =−0.16, p = 0.008), but no significant correlation was found between Emean and pancreatic lipomatosis ( r =−0.01, p = 0.881). The discriminant ability of Emean to pancreatic fibrosis stage F1-F2, F2-F3, acinar atrophy stage A0-A1, A1-A2, and stromal edema stage E0-E1 was also significant (all p < 0.050; Fig. , Supplementary Table 6). A significant correlation was also found between POPF grade and pancreatic fibrosis ( r =−0.26, p < 0.001) and acinar atrophy ( r =−0.20, p < 0.001), while the correlation of POPF with pancreatic lipomatosis and stromal oedema was not significant (both p > 0.050). Risk factors of the occurrence of POPF For the training group, the multivariate logistic analysis indicated that the higher BMI [odds ratio (OR) = 1.19, p = 0.002], non-dilated pancreatic duct (OR = 0.24, p = 0.001), and lower Emean (OR = 0.49, p < 0.001) were the independent risk factors of POPF occurrence (Table ; Supplementary Table 7). Accordingly, a predictive model was built: In the model, P POPF represented the predicted POPF incidence. BMI was expressed in kg/m². DMPD referred to the pancreatic duct status, with dilation recorded as 1 and non-dilation as 0. Emean was the 2D-SWE measured pancreatic stiffness expressed in kPa. The intercept was 1.28, and the β for BMI, DMPD, and Emean was 0.17, −1.42, and − 0.72, respectively. All VIF values are very close to 1 (Emean: 1.05; BMI: 1.04; pancreatic duct dilation: 1.02), indicating an absence of concerning multicollinearity among the predictor variables. Furthermore, tests for two-way interactions between Emean, pancreatic duct dilation, and BMI revealed no statistically significant interactions (all p > 0.050), supporting the adequacy of the main effects model. Moreover, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess the impact of excluding patients with failed 2D-SWE measurements. In the worst-case scenario, OR was 0.60 (95% CI: 0.51–0.71, p < 0.001), while in the best-case scenario, the OR was 0.56 (95% CI: 0.46–0.67, p < 0.001), indicating the robustness of the findings regarding Emean. Additionally, the IDI analysis confirmed that the inclusion of Emean significantly enhanced the model’s performance (IDI: 0.17, 95% CI: 0.12–0.22, p < 0.001). Performance of the model in predicting POPF occurrence The Hosmer–Lemeshow test indicated good calibration of the predictive model, with p = 0.879 in the training group, p = 0.805 in the validation group, and p = 0.904 in the total cohort. In both groups, the P POPF model effectively discriminated POPF occurrence [AUC (95% CI) = 0.84 (0.79–0.89), p < 0.001 in the training group and AUC (95% CI) = 0.81 (0.82–0.90), p < 0.001 in the validation group]. Calibration plots of each group was shown in Supplementary Fig. 2 and the decision-curve analysis was shown in Supplementary Fig. 3. The model also distinguished CR-POPF and grade C POPF occurrence (all p < 0.050; Fig. ; Table ). According to the model, the Emean ranges corresponding to different probabilities of developing POPF were calculated under different BMI and the status of pancreatic duct dilation (Table ). Moreover, in the five-fold cross-validation, the model achieved an average AUC of 0.82 (standard deviation 0.06; range 0.73–0.89), which was close to the original AUC of 0.83 calculated from the full dataset. The small reduction in AUC suggests minimal overfitting and good internal stability of the model. Moreover, the model showed significant associations with post-operative infection ( r = 0.16, p = 0.005), longer hospital stay ( r = 0.12, p = 0.034), and higher 1-month readmission rates ( r = 0.14, p = 0.014). As regards POPF occurrence, there were significant differences among different types of pancreatectomy and surgical techniques (all p < 0.050; Supplementary Table 8, Supplementary Table 9); while among the minimally invasive surgeries, there was no significant difference between laparoscopic and robotic surgeries ( p > 0.050). ROC analysis was thus performed to investigate the performance of the model to predict POPF across surgical procedures. Accordingly, the model could distinguish between POPF grades across different surgical techniques (all AUC > 0.70, p < 0.050; Supplementary Table 10). As

As regards POPF occurrence, there were significant differences among different types of pancreatectomy and surgical techniques (all p < 0.050; Supplementary Table 8, Supplementary Table 9); while among the minimally invasive surgeries, there was no significant difference between laparoscopic and robotic surgeries ( p > 0.050). ROC analysis was thus performed to investigate the performance of the model to predict POPF across surgical procedures. Accordingly, the model could distinguish between POPF grades across different surgical techniques (all AUC > 0.70, p < 0.050; Supplementary Table 10). As regards pancreatectomy type, the model showed significant discrimination between POPF grades in PD surgery (all AUC > 0.80, p < 0.050). However, in DP surgery, the model only distinguished POPF and CR-POPF occurrence (both AUC > 0.80, p < 0.050), with no significant ability to differentiate grade C POPF ( p = 0.984). Discussion This study demonstrates that lower Emean is significantly associated with an increased risk of POPF. The histological analysis provides an explanation for this association, confirming that Emean reflects key histological features, including pancreatic fibrosis and acinar atrophy. One of the key innovations of the study is the development of a pre-operative predictive model that incorporates 2D-SWE, BMI, and pancreatic duct dilation, which was internally validated for its robustness. Furthermore, this study includes a large, diverse cohort that spans various pancreatic diseases and surgical procedures, enhancing the generalizability of our findings. These highlight the broader applicability of 2D-SWE in POPF risk prediction and underscore its value as a non-invasive, pre-operative assessment tool. Collectively, this study contributes to a deeper mechanistic understanding of pancreatic 2D-SWE and extends its clinical utility in the peri-operative setting. Consistent with previous studies, this study indicated that those with softer pancreatic tissue were more likely to develop higher-grade POPF [ , , , ]. Compared to intra-operative texture, magnetic resonance elastography, endoscopic ultrasound elastography, and pancreatic parenchymal fibrosis, 2D-SWE offers a convenient, non-invasive, objective, and quantitative assessment of pancreas stiffness. A possible reason for the soft pancreas’s association with the higher POPF occurrence was that the tissue might be more susceptible to injury during surgical manipulation and have a low suture-holding capacity [ – ]. Also, in the surgery, the soft tissue might have technical difficulty in sealing off a delicate, friable transection margin [ ]. Another reason for the elevated POPF occurrence, as regards the histological basis, might be the lower fibrosis degree and the higher content of pancreatic lobules in the soft pancreas. The lobules could produce more pancreatic juice, which is rich in proteolytic enzymes and could increase the risk of pancreaticoenteric anastomosis disruption [ , , – ]. Our analysis of pancreatic histological features and POPF supports this hypothesis: pancreatic fibrosis and acinar atrophy may underlie the predictive ability of 2D-SWE to POPF. However, Emean was not only correlated with pancreatic fibrosis and acinar atrophy but also negatively correlated with stromal oedema. Stromal oedema also showed a significant association with pancreatic stiffness and POPF in this study. Although the underlying mechanism remains uncertain, it may reflect inflammatory or reactive changes influencing tissue stiffness. Given the lack of prior evidence, this finding should be interpreted cautiously and warrants further investigation in future histopathological and imaging studies. The semi-quantitative histological scoring system used in this study is not internationally standardised, and potential intra- and inter-observer variability cannot be excluded. Future studies are warranted to validate the reproducibility of pancreatic histological assessment across observers. Similar to previous studies, this research found that pancreatic duct dilation and BMI also influenced POPF [ , , ]. The narrow pancreatic duct might complicate the anastomosis creation [ ]. Also, the non-dilated pancreatic duct might be susceptible to occlusion or dehiscence in the duct-to-mucosa anastomosis procedure in partial pancreatectomy, and the obstructed pancreatic juice in the duct may erode the pancreatic intestinal anastomosis [ ]. However, the assessment of pancreatic duct status was necessarily limited to a binary classification rather than a continuous diameter measurement. This was due to the inherent difficulty in obtaining precise millimeter measurements from imaging for non-dilated or minimally dilated ducts, alongside the lack of a universally accepted multi-category classification. While our binary classification approach ensures clinical practicality, it may result in some loss of information. Moreover, the association between BMI and POPF might result from the visceral fat hindering operative exposure and obscuring the anatomical structures, particularly the vessels [ ]. However, previous studies suggested that BMI might affect the success rate of pancreatic 2D-SWE examination [ ]. Since this study only included patients with successful 2D-SWE examinations (most of them had normal BMI), factors influencing POPF in those with abnormal BMI remain to be explored. Moreover, the association between BMI and POPF might result from the visceral fat hindering operative exposure and obscuring the anatomical structures, particularly the vessels [ ]. However, previous studies suggested that BMI might affect the success rate of pancreatic 2D-SWE examination [ ]. Since this study only included patients with successful 2D-SWE examinations (most of them had normal BMI), factors influencing POPF in those with abnormal BMI remain to be explored. Moreover, potential confounders such as smoking, alcohol consumption, diabetes, and nutritional status may influence the pancreas and thus affect the POPF risk. In our analysis, these factors showed no significant associations with POPF, but their binary classification in our data without quantitative assessment may have introduced residual confounding. Consistent with previous studies [ , ], this study showed that the POPF grade varied across different surgical types. However, the model built in this study showed limited predictive performance for grade C POPF. Advanced approaches such as penalised regression or resampling could potentially address class imbalance and enhance prediction in future studies. However, given the small number of grade C cases, applying such methods might lead to overfitting. The model built in this study should be further refined and externally validated in larger, multicenter cohorts. In addition, this study found no significant differences in POPF occurrence rates across different surgical types or surgeons. However, the selection of surgeons and surgical types was greatly influenced by socioeconomic and subjective factors; thus, further studies were warranted. Moreover, in our analysis, surgeon experience was not significantly associated with POPF occurrence, though surgical expertise is often considered an important determinant of postoperative outcomes. However, all operations were performed by surgeons from the same experienced team. This limited variability may have obscured potential effects of surgical expertise, and future multicenter studies with broader operator diversity are needed to confirm these findings. Previous studies in healthy volunteers have shown that pancreatic 2D-SWE measurements demonstrate the best intra- and inter-operator reproducibility in the pancreatic body and that Emean does not differ significantly between the head and body, but is markedly higher in the tail [ ]. Based on these findings, the pancreatic body was prioritised as the preferred measurement site in this study, followed by the head when the body was not suitable. Consequently, all 2D-SWE measurements in this cohort were obtained from the pancreatic head and body, with no tail measurements performed. In our patient population, one of the main factors influencing the measurement site was the location of the lesion. Patients with lesions involving the pancreatic body were relatively less likely to be included, as reliable 2D-SWE acquisition was more challenging in such cases. However, the relationship between the pre-operative measurement site and the subsequent surgical resection line remains to be clarified. In addition, operator judgment and imaging feasibility may also have influenced site selection to some extent, potentially introducing variability. Moreover, although earlier studies reported acceptable inter- and intra-operator reproducibility [ , ], we acknowledge that our findings warrant further large-scale, multicenter verification regarding the inter- and intra-operator reproducibility. The present study still had other limitations. First, the study cohort was heterogeneous, including patients with both pancreatic and periampullary diseases who underwent different types of partial pancreatectomy. This design reflected real-world surgical practice, where POPF risk assessment is clinically relevant across these types of disease. However, inherent variations in histological characteristics and surgical approaches among disease categories were unavoidable, introducing potential confounding. Moreover, the limited number of patients within subgroups for each specific disease and surgical procedure reduced the statistical power for detailed stratified analyses. Second, though different surgical types were analysed, data on several technically important surgical factors (such as pancreatic gland thickness, gland texture, specific stump closure or anastomotic techniques, and the use of drains or stents) were not consistently available for analysis. The absence of these variables introduces the potential for residual confounding, and future prospective studies should aim to incorporate them. Third, in this study, both the training and validation groups were derived from the same centre and surgical team; the generalizability of our conclusions to other institutions, equipment, or operators remains uncertain. External validation in prospective, multicenter studies is warranted to confirm its broader applicability. Fourth, the absence of histological data in 24 patients due to the insufficient pancreatic parenchyma sample may have introduced potential selection bias, and this limitation should be considered when interpreting the histological findings. Fifth, patients who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy were excluded due to substantial heterogeneity and incomplete documentation of treatment regimens, which prevented reliable assessment of its potential impact on pancreatic 2D-SWE and post-operative outcomes. Sixth, only patients with successful 2D-SWE examinations were included, while 39 patients failed. This inclusion criterion may have introduced selection bias, and the predictive factors

prospective, multicenter studies is warranted to confirm its broader applicability. Fourth, the absence of histological data in 24 patients due to the insufficient pancreatic parenchyma sample may have introduced potential selection bias, and this limitation should be considered when interpreting the histological findings. Fifth, patients who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy were excluded due to substantial heterogeneity and incomplete documentation of treatment regimens, which prevented reliable assessment of its potential impact on pancreatic 2D-SWE and post-operative outcomes. Sixth, only patients with successful 2D-SWE examinations were included, while 39 patients failed. This inclusion criterion may have introduced selection bias, and the predictive factors of POPF in such technically challenging cases warrant further investigation. Furthermore, a direct comparison with established POPF risk scores, such as the Fistula Risk Score [ , ], was not feasible due to the pre-operative design of our study, which did not collect intra-operative data like pancreatic gland texture. Such a comparison is necessary to fully contextualize the clinical utility of our model, and it might be one key objective for future studies. Additionally, the relationship between Emean and post-operative pancreatitis was not systematically evaluated in this study due to the difficulty in diagnosis of pancreatitis. The necessary biochemical data (post-operative amylase and lipase levels) [ , ] were not routinely collected in our centre, as testing was triggered by clinical symptoms, and thus an exploratory analysis regarding post-operative pancreatitis is not considered reliable. Investigating the potential of 2D-SWE to predict post-operative pancreatitis remains an important area for future prospective studies that incorporate systematic post-operative monitoring. Conclusions The lower pancreatic 2D-SWE measurements were associated with a higher risk of developing POPF, and the histological basis for this may lie in 2D-SWE’s correlation with pancreatic fibrosis and acinar atrophy. The present study developed a pre-operative predictive model for POPF using pancreatic 2D-SWE measurements, BMI, and the presence of pancreatic duct dilation, which could predict POPF risk across varying severity levels and was applicable to different surgical types.
